name: Duchy of Lorraine
region: Eastern France / Western Holy Roman Empire border zone
hover_description: Lorraine: Nicolas Rémy prosecuted 800+ witches 1576–1606. The 'Lotharingian corridor' — densest execution zone in Europe alongside the German territories.
panel_description:
The Duchy of Lorraine occupied the border zone between France and the Holy Roman Empire, and its prosecution record between 1576 and 1631 places it among the most intensive execution zones in the whole of Europe. Nicolas Rémy, the duchy's attorney-general (procureur général), claimed personal responsibility for sentencing more than 800 accused to death between 1576 and 1606; his compilation of their testimony, Demonolatry (1595; Daemonolatreiae libri tres), became one of the most widely-read Continental demonological texts and ranks alongside del Río's Disquisitiones Magicae and de Lancre's Tableau as a systematic synthesis built directly from confessional evidence obtained in actual prosecutions.

  Robin Briggs's Witches and Neighbours (1996), based on sustained archival research into the surviving Lorraine trial records, is the defining historiographical study of the duchy's prosecution. Briggs's analysis demonstrates that Lorraine witch accusations were not products of elite panic or institutional pressure from above but were generated at the village level through the accumulated logic of neighborly suspicion: charity refusals, livestock illness, children's ailments, and disputed boundaries created long-running community tensions that eventually issued in formal accusation. The accused typically had been suspected by their neighbors for years or decades before any judicial proceeding began; what Briggs documents is a distinctly French regional pattern of community-driven prosecution that differed significantly from the institutional superhunts of the adjacent German Prince-Bishoprics.

  The 'Lotharingian corridor' — the execution zone extending through the duchy into neighboring Alsace, Franche-Comté, and Luxembourg — represents, alongside the German territories, the densest witchcraft execution geography in Europe. Behringer estimates between 3,000 and 5,000 total executions for the broader corridor. Stuart Clark, in Thinking with Demons (1997), analyzes Rémy's Demonolatry within the intellectual history of demonological naturalism: Rémy presented his accumulated trial evidence as an empirical natural history of diabolic activity, a rhetorical strategy that cast prosecution as rational inquiry rather than theological assertion, and that positioned the confessional record as equivalent in epistemological standing to contemporary natural-historical observation.
administrative_context: The Duchy of Lorraine occupied the border zone between France and the Holy Roman Empire, combining French legal culture with proximity to the German prosecutorial tradition. Its secular duke wielded criminal jurisdiction without the complex appeals structure of the Empire proper, enabling sustained high-intensity prosecution.
witchcraft_trials_significance: Lorraine was the most intensive prosecution zone in the French cultural sphere and one of the most intensive in Europe. Nicolas Rémy, the duchy's attorney-general (procureur général), claimed to have personally sentenced over 800 witches to death between 1576 and 1606. His compilation of their confessions, Demonolatry (1595), became one of the most widely-read Continental demonological texts. Lorraine exemplified the 'Lotharingian corridor' of intensive prosecution that included Franche-Comté, Luxembourg, and the Rhineland border zone.

key_magistrates.name: Nicolas Rémy
key_magistrates.contribution_to_trials: Prosecuted 800+ witches; systematized confessional evidence in Demonolatry (1595); provided judicial framework for sustained high-intensity prosecution

persecution_timeline.1576–1590: Initial sustained prosecution under Rémy's direction
persecution_timeline.1590–1606: Peak intensity; Rémy's Demonolatry (1595) systematizes the accumulated confessional evidence
persecution_timeline.1607–1660: Continued prosecution after Rémy's death; Lorraine remained one of the most active prosecution zones in Europe

affected_population.geographic_extent: Duchy of Lorraine, including rural villages and urban centers along the Moselle
affected_population.social_reach: Primarily rural accused; predominantly female; concentrated in village-level accusation
affected_population.mortality_impact: 800+ under Rémy alone (1576–1606); total prosecution losses across the full period were substantially higher

scholarly_analysis.clark_perspective: Clark uses Lorraine and Rémy as a primary case study in the 'naturalistic' strand of demonological thinking — Rémy's Demonolatry emphasized the consistency of confessional evidence as natural-historical proof of diabolic reality, parallel to Glanvill's later use of Baconian methodology.
scholarly_analysis.hutton_perspective: Lorraine exemplifies the regional concentration of persecution in the 'Lotharingian corridor' — the border zone where French legal culture, German prosecutorial intensity, and proximity to the Rhineland superhunts combined to create the highest execution density in Europe.
scholarly_analysis.ginzburg_perspective: Lorraine's high prosecution volume was sustained by the same torture-confession-denunciation dynamic Ginzburg analyzes, but Rémy's self-conscious compilation of confessional evidence (Demonolatry) also illustrates how inquisitorial testimony was converted into systematic demonological argument.

legacy_and_historiographical_importance: Lorraine's significance is primarily through Nicolas Rémy: his Demonolatry (1595) is one of the three major systematic demonological compilations (alongside del Río's Disquisitiones and de Lancre's Tableau) based directly on confessional testimony from actual prosecutions. Lorraine is therefore both an execution site and a primary source generator for the demonological literature.
primary_sources: Nicolas Rémy, Demonolatry (Nancy/Lyon, 1595); Lorraine ducal archives; trial records analyzed in Robin Briggs, Witches and Neighbours (1996)
source_method: Robin Briggs, Witches and Neighbours (1996); Stuart Clark, Thinking with Demons (1997/2001); Brian Levack, The Witch-Hunt in Early Modern Europe; primary source: Nicolas Rémy, Demonolatry (1595)
